A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
reconcile
Check that separate records agree.
corroborate
Support a claim using another source.
custody
Responsibility for holding a document safely.
cryptic
Difficult to understand from limited wording.
authenticate
Establish that an item is genuine.
lawful disclosure
Sharing information as permitted by law.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

By Wednesday morning, the storage trail had acquired something it had lacked until then: a plausible, documented explanation for the cryptic index notation. Fiona telephoned with the company's findings. Staff had checked the old note marked “Location changed”. The phrase referred to a 2013 warehouse reorganisation during which holdings had been transferred between premises and their location codes altered. It did not, in itself, document the contents of any particular carton.

“Does that mean you have found the authorisation register?” Emma asked.

“Not yet,” Fiona said. “The index connects the old box number to a newer location code. It doesn't describe what is inside.”

A subsequent stock-check sheet dated 2014 supplied another reference point. Beside the new code was a tick and a date. Fiona cautioned that a mark on an inventory supported a recordkeeping claim, not the survival or completeness of every document supposedly stored there.

Sarah was excited when Emma explained the news. “They must have the register, then.”

“They may have the box,” Emma answered. “Even that needs a physical check. We can't say the register is there.”

Fiona had asked the company to search its current shelves. Because the records belonged to the trust and could contain private student information, Emma could not visit the warehouse or inspect the box herself.

While she waited, she looked again at the four headings in her notebook: request, authorisation, transfer and receipt. If the missing book existed, it might show who had approved unusual payments. It would not, on its own, prove that the bank had sent the money.

Helen Ward sent a short message. Her cousin had nothing more to share at present. Emma thanked her. She would not treat an absent bank statement as evidence of a missing grant.

In the afternoon Fiona called again. The warehouse team had found a box carrying the newer location code. Its label included the old reference from the trust's transfer list. The seal was dusty but unbroken, according to the warehouse worker.

“So it is the right box?” Emma asked.

“It may be. We need to compare the references and check the contents properly. The company hasn't opened it.”

The physical discovery was stronger than the uncorroborated catalogue entry, yet the chain of identification still rested on labels and staff reports rather than a verified contents inventory. Emma asked Fiona to ensure that anyone opening it recorded what was found, including any pages missing or damaged. She also asked that student details remain private.

Late that evening Fiona sent a final email. The trust and the storage company had agreed to arrange a supervised examination. Their plan was to reconcile the old and new references, document the condition and contents on opening, and separate verification from the later decision about lawful disclosure.

Sarah read the message and smiled. “Tomorrow we might finally learn who signed.”

“Maybe,” Emma said. “First we find out whether the book is inside.”

She closed her notebook, then opened it once more and wrote: Found a possible box. Not yet found the truth.
